metadata.title: How much do 15-year-olds learn over one year of schooling? An international comparison based on PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analysis uses PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 microdata for 18 countries/economies, with inference accounting for PISA’s complex two-stage sampling design (schools, then students). The paper states that all statistical inference is computed using resampling methods and that replicate weights are provided with PISA databases; it also notes the use of the Stata package repest to implement this. The regressions are estimated with standard errors that account for clustering and the sampling design, but the manuscript does not name a specific weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because this is an instrumental-variables framework rather than ML prediction, the key weighting requirement is to use PISA replicate weights (and the associated variance estimation approach) when estimating standard errors and confidence intervals for the grade-and-age effects.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an official IEA/OECD technical report or assessment framework. It describes sampling, scaling, and instrument design rather than student-level predictive modeling. Plausible values are therefore not applicable to the document's primary analytic purpose; any missing-data discussion refers to fieldwork or scaling procedures, not a single ML imputation strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2015 and/or PISA 2018 data for 18 countries/economies where the PISA cohort is expected to be found in two distinct grades due to school-entry regulations. It restricts to students aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months (PISA eligible population) and uses only countries where the cut-off date for first-grade enrolment acts as a binding constraint and is positively related to actual grade; it excludes eight countries with very open enrolment policies and excludes the United Kingdom, Scotland, and Austria from the main analysis. For each country, it further restricts the estimation sample by excluding birth months that would violate the identification assumptions (e.g., excluding students born in the cut-off month for Costa Rica and Baku; excluding all months between the earliest and latest local cut-off for Germany and Switzerland; excluding June–August for the Czech Republic and Slovak Republic; and dropping 13 observations in Chinese Taipei to restrict the PISA cohort to a 12-month birth window). For Albania and Korea, the estimation sample does not include PISA 2015 data due to missing key controls (Albania) or differing primary school cut-off dates across cohorts (Korea).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD study quantifies typical learning gains over one school year for 15-year-olds using PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 microdata in 18 countries/economies. Because PISA is cross-sectional, the authors exploit school-entry regulations to create an instrumental-variables design that uses expected grade (from month of birth) to identify the grade-and-age effect, under local linearity assumptions for age effects. The analysis uses multiply imputed test scores (plausible values) and reports standard errors that account for clustering and the complex sampling design via PISA replicate weights. Across countries, the average grade-and-age learning gain is about 19 score points (≈0.2 SD) in mathematics, reading, and science, with wide country-level confidence intervals and stronger gains in higher-income contexts. The estimates are local average treatment effects for “compliers” near cut-offs, so they provide benchmarks rather than fully generalizable causal effects for all students.
